title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
description: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom
body: Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option.""He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said."What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had."For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that."Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

schema.headline: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion

title: LIV Golf: Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell confirms exit
description: Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf. The 2010 US Open winner, 47, announced
body: Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf. The 2010 US Open winner, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027.Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week. England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition. Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed.Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022.The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025."I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell. "I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey."I look forward to the next chapter in my career."Earlier this year, McDowell told BBC Sport NI he had held "really positive" talks about returning to the DP World Tour next season, adding he was "lucky to have that option".

schema.headline: LIV Golf: Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell confirms exit

title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
description: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her
body: Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example."She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020."Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family. That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.There was also criticism levelled at Meghan in December 2025 when her father was in hospital in the Philippines, undergoing the amputation of his leg. "I don't want to die estranged from Meghan. I want to meet my grandkids. It might be nice to meet her husband too," Markle told the Mail on Sunday at the time. There was a media storm about whether Meghan was going to reach out to her father, culminating in a letter being delivered from her to her father, which at the time was assumed to be well-wishes.But that whole episode now looks different with the benefit of hindsight. That letter was a much more fraught affair. It revealed that Meghan knew about the allegations against her father. We now understand that Meghan was telling him he would never see his grandchildren.Thomas Markle has strongly denied all the allegations against him, saying they are "sick lies" which are trying to destroy his reputation.His daughter Samantha Markle has also rejected the claims, saying the stories are "fake news" and "clickbait". "There will be no legal action against my dad with no evidence in so many flimsy stories and my dad never had access to any such content and was in the hospital most of the time that he was there," she wrote on X on Sunday.Samantha also challenges the credibility of the letter written by her mother, Roslyn Loveless, which was shared with Meghan in 2019 and contained details of allegations of sexual abuse against Thomas Markle. When you look through photos of Meghan at events over the last seven years, you wonder what was going on behind the familiar smile.Those years have seen Netflix films, a tell-all memoir by Prince Harry, cookery series, podcasts and TV interviews. But a hidden narrative has been running in the background.Meghan's supporters have pointed to other factors in how she has been treated, with racism and sexism part of that toxic mix.But maybe there was also a sense of not knowing the authentic person behind the polished Brand Meghan.On Instagram, she has curated her life to look idyllic, but perhaps she'll get a more generous hearing now that her back story is as messy and imperfect as everyone else's.It could still be an uphill struggle to become more popular, beyond her own vocal, core group of supporters.A survey from YouGov earlier this month found 22% of people had a positive view of Meghan, compared with 49% who dislike her.That suggests there is still some way to go before Meghan fully wins the trust of the public. Fascination, yes. But affection, not always.For the British public, Californian Meghan hasn't always translated well.But perhaps this complex, still developing story - and the light it sheds on previous years - might mean there's a more rounded view of her in the future.

schema.headline: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?

title: Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo
description: Image source, RBGEImage caption, Richard Baines worked at Logan Botanic Garden near StranraerByNichola Rutherford Reporting fromCastle Douglas and Lor
body: Image source, RBGEImage caption, Richard Baines worked at Logan Botanic Garden near StranraerByNichola Rutherford Reporting fromCastle Douglas and Lori CarnochanBBC ScotlandReporting fromLogan Botanic GardenTributes have been paid to a man who died after being hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway. Richard Baines, 60, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Stranraer, died during Storm Boelo on Sunday morning. It is understood that he was walking near his home in Mid Kelton, just outside Castle Douglas, when the accident happened.David Knott, director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh, said they were "desperately sad, devastated" by the news."He had a warmth, a genuine sense of humour, he always made time for individuals and that's one of the tributes that has been said many times this morning," Knott told BBC Scotland News.  "He always found time for his colleagues. And he was always very supportive in providing opportunities for the next generation of horticulturalists. He was a very genuine and warm human being."Logan Botanic Garden is home to a range of exotic plants as it benefits from the warming influence of the Gulf Stream. It is one of four Scottish gardens run by the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. Knott said Baines came up with the description of Logan as "Scotland's most exotic garden" and worked hard to promote both the garden and the south-west of Scotland.Image source, RBGEImage caption, Baines described Logan as "Scotland's most exotic garden"Knott said his colleague would be remembered for his "passion and enthusiasm for plants" and for significantly expanding the plant collection at Logan. During his tenure, he was primarily responsible for significant developments including the first public conservatory to be powered by green energy in the UK. Baines also participated and led fieldwork in China, the Canary Islands and Vietnam, from where seven plant species new to science were catalogued. "Richard's contribution as an enthusiastic plantsman and curator at Logan and to the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh's wider work and culture has been immeasurable, and he will be deeply missed by many," Knott said. Image caption, The accident happened at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and GallowayDumfries and Galloway MSP Finlay Carson also paid tribute to Baines, a former school friend."Richard was a remarkable gentleman and a good friend to many, always ready with a warm smile, a kind word and an infectious enthusiasm for life," he said.The Scottish Conservative MSP said that Baines' work at Logan Botanic Garden had earned him national recognition."His expertise, commitment and achievements brought credit not only to his profession but to Galloway as well," he added.Baines died as Storm Boelo swept across Scotland, causing flooding, travel disruption and power cuts over the weekend and into Monday.The wind picked up on Saturday and an amber warning was in place from Saturday night. Galloway Mountain Rescue Team (GMRT) said they had responded to "one of the most gruelling callouts our team had faced in recent history" on Saturday. They were called to Curleywee in the Minigaff Hills to help a runner who was injured while taking part in the OMM mountain challenge. In a post on Facebook, external, they said 10 members of their team pushed through "torrential rain, severe wind and unforgiving boggy ground" to reach the casualty.A coastguard helicopter had to turn back due to the deteriorating weather. The team said they had to carry the casualty off the hill, with the help of members of the OMM safety team, before handing the runner to the Scottish Ambulance Service. OMM has faced some criticism on social media for allowing the run to go ahead in the poor weather. A spokesperson said the course was closed and all competitors accounted for before the amber wind warning took effect at 21:00 on Saturday. "The event team continually assessed the mountain weather forecast in the build-up to and throughout the event, with competitor safety guiding every decision," they added. The spokesperson said they were grateful for the "understanding and support" shown as the event was adapted to the forecast conditions. They said they would be making as a donation to GMRT, as is usual practice at OMM events whether or not a callout takes place.

schema.headline: Tributes paid to man killed by falling tree in Storm Boelo

title: Rapper Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
description: Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month.The Ameri
body: Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month.The American star played to a crowd of up to 13,000 at the city's 3Arena, having promised "many incredible surprise guests" on the bill for the sold-out show.The artist, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, announced the tour days after being dropped from Sheeran's Loop Tour after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.He was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches, including referring to the death toll from Israel's military action in Gaza as a genocide - a claim that Israel rejects.Sheeran later said that the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by himself.Among the acts who performed at Macklemore's Dublin show were singer-songwriter Hozier, rap trio Kneecap and folk band Beoga, who had also performed on Sheeran's tour.Macklemore has said that proceeds from his Free Palestine tour will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.He will perform in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday.The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israel says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.The controversy began when Macklemore, performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in New Jersey in early September, said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US.The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration.Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

schema.headline: Rapper Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout

title: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
description: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba corresp
body: Figure caption, Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exileByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondentDriving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration,  which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.Now, it appears, it is."Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."Image caption, Gregory Noriega"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap."She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel.  "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared." Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.  Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty. He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined. The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of  President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro. The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides. When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.Image source, Getty ImagesThe Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil. The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon."The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country.""The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.Image caption, Political analyst Beningno AlarconFor instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution. Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.Image caption, Young supporters of Maria MachadoHaving made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has  Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy. Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing. Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.Figure caption, Watch:  December 2025 - BBC interview Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina MachadoAdditional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

schema.headline: María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump

title: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around
description: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particu
body: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off"."Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult. While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback. Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights."It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media."It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement."Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration."I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed."We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

schema.headline: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around

title: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time
description: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth con
body: Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas has won the Ballon d'Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time, keeping the prize in Spanish hands for a sixth consecutive year.Putellas, 32, captained Barcelona to Champions League glory as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women's Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July.She joins Spain team-mate Aitana Bonmati on three Ballon d'Or Feminin crowns - her former Barcelona colleague won the award in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas did so in 2021 and 2022.The past six Ballons d'Or have been won by the Spanish pair, with Norway's Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spaniards to claim the prize.Putellas' latest victory caps a remarkable return to the pinnacle of world football after suffering a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in 2022."All the boys and girls around the world - if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn't matter if you're a boy or if you're a girl," Putellas said."Doesn't matter where you come from. Don't listen if someone tells you, you can't do it. Believe in yourself."She collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across Fifa's top-50 ranked countries, with Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor coming second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third.Meanwhile, England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or, becoming the first English player to do so since Michael Owen in 2001.While Barcelona are always overwhelming favourites to win the three competitions on offer in Spain, Putellas' performances last season showed that she is still among the world's elite.Nicknamed 'La Reina' - meaning the queen - Putellas scored 21 goals and provided 13 assists in all competitions, ranking her third and second respectively among players across Europe's top five leagues.Seven of those goals came in the Women's Champions League as Barcelona claimed a fourth continental title in six seasons.Only Pernille Harder (eight), Alessia Russo (nine) and Ewa Pajor (11) scored more, all of whom are strikers by trade.But Putellas' contributions to Barcelona's attacking play went far beyond scoring goals herself.In Liga F - which Barcelona won for a seventh consecutive season - she finished joint-sixth for assists (seven) and fourth for open-play chances created (40).Across Europe's top five leagues, only Claudia Pina (199), Vicky Lopez (183) and Georgia Stanway (168) recorded more sequence involvements ending in an open-play shot than Putellas (151).In all competitions, she created more chances (89, 19 of which were big chances) and completed more passes ending in the final third (965) than any other player in Liga F, the Champions League, Copa de la Reina and Supercopa de Espana.Only Bayern Munich's Klara Buhl created as many chances as Putellas in the Champions League last season (36), the most by a player in a single edition of the competition since Caroline Graham Hansen in 2021-22 (38).Putellas was born and grew up in the Catalan municipality of Mollet del Valles, about 12 miles north-east of Barcelona.She began playing football in the street, and soon became a Barcelona fan and a regular attendee at Camp Nou.With matches always on the TV at home, former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta and Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho quickly became her idols.After attending a summer football camp run by Xavi and playing for local side CE Sabadell, Putellas spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy.Spells at Espanyol and Levante followed the disbandment of her girls team, before she eventually returned to Barca in 2012.Cue the start of a 14-year career with her childhood club during which she won 38 trophies, including 10 league titles and four European cups.But after winning the Ballon d'Or for the first time in 2021, one of the toughest moments of Putellas' career came when she suffered an ACL injury on the eve of Euro 2022, ruling her out of the tournament.Though she retained the Ballon d'Or later that year, it took a while for her to return to her best level. Playing only a bit-part role in Spain's triumphant 2023 World Cup campaign would have stung.After scoring in the 2024 Champions League final and improving further the following season, in 2025-26 she shouldered much of Barcelona's creative burden as Aitana Bonmati missed five months through injury and ended the season a quadruple winner.If that was not enough, the midfielder scored twice in a 4-0 thrashing of England in June that secured Spain's place at the 2027 World Cup at the Lionesses' expense.With her contract at Barcelona expiring and keen for a fresh challenge, Putellas made the decision to leave her childhood club. She, and her fans, were distraught.She had several offers from England, Mexico and the United States, but joined the ambitious project of US billionaire Michelle Kang at London City Lionesses in July."I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player," Putellas told BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast in August.With three goals and one assist in seven WSL games for her new club, it is clear Putellas is still deserving of her nickname.

schema.headline: Ballon d'Or Feminin: Alexia Putellas wins award for record-equalling third time

title: Man Utd: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on list if Michael Carrick sacked
description: Michael Carrick has left Manchester United's training ground following talks over his future, with Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann emerging as early
body: Michael Carrick has left Manchester United's training ground following talks over his future, with Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann emerging as early contenders to replace him if he is sacked.Carrick's position at Old Trafford is under major threat following the club's poor start to the season, with work towards identifying his successor believed to be ongoing.It is understood Howe and Nagelsmann both feature prominently on the list of candidates the club has explored to potentially replace him, and that both managers are aware of United's interest.Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.Howe, Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte - who is interested in the job - are out of work, making their potential appointments easier.Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Newcastle boss Howe is fully open to joining United if Carrick loses his job.Nagelsmann is available after leaving his job as Germany head coach after the World Cup, while Conte - who has also been linked with Juventus - is open to returning to football after leaving Napoli in May.Carrick left United's Carrington training ground at around 17:00 GMT on Monday.Should he be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title.Here, BBC Sport takes a closer look at the contenders who could be up for the job.

schema.headline: Man Utd: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on list if Michael Carrick sacked

title: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'
description: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma Crew
body: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma CrewChancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.Chloe's biggest worry is the cost of living. Her husband passed away four years ago and she's bringing up their 16-year-old son alone.She's very grateful the rent for her south London maisonette is subsidised through a housing association, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."Her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity."We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families."I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.   "Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax. He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently. He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."'I get £338 UC per month. I'm trying my best'Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college. The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers."I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump."The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year."I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors."If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her. "It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'

title: Healey pledges cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package
description: Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.Healey said that the ongoing wars in Iran a
body: Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional £19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.Healey said that the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs". "We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added.Other measures the government announced include:Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above thatAllowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism insteadGiving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the periodAnd rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easierThe government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. As first reported in The Sun, the 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn't mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren't fair."If you're a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket."But the Conservatives said Burnham's "everyday fixes" have already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

schema.headline: Healey pledges cheaper marmalade and gherkins in pre-Budget package

title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
description: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were rel
body: Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the White House's immigration stance. Trump won the support of 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, a Pew study found.In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons". "In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said. "I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media. Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump. Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants. "I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote."I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added. Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event. When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops. "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

schema.headline: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting

title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO
description: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blo
body: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance"."In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields."We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

schema.headline: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of major IPO

title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."ByIan YoungsCulture reporte
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, James Bourne: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."ByIan YoungsCulture reporterBusted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bourne with his Busted bandmates Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in 2023"Wow, what the hell happened?" James wrote on Monday. "One minute you're heading out on tour, the next thing you know you're on the bench and out of the game."My condition was serious and the doctors told me I had a few years left to live."I'm happy to share now that my youngest brother, Chris, who stepped in for me on tour last year, has saved my life yet again. This time quite literally by donating me one of his kidneys."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chris Bourne went on tour with Busted after his brother was forced to drop outJames continued: "I can't believe how much better I'm starting to feel already."I'm still going to need some time, but I wanted you to know that we're both recovering from surgery just fine. My brother is a hero."Chris posted his own message on X saying simply: "We did it brother."Bourne has not given any more details of his condition.Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Busted had eight top 10 hits in the UK between 2002 and 2004The guitarist, vocalist and songwriter shot to fame with Charlie Simpson and Matt Willis in Busted in the early 2000s, and the trio had hits including What I Go To School For, Year 3000 and Crashed the Wedding.They scored four number one singles in the UK before splitting up in 2005. In 2013, Bourne and Willis teamed up with McFly to make McBusted, before Simpson rejoined Busted for a full reunion in 2015.Bourne has written songs for McFly and 5 Seconds of Summer, and also fronted his own band, Son of Dork. He recently released the music from his stage musical Murder at the Gates.

schema.headline: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation

title: Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
description: In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan."The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and comm
body: In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan."The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media.It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".Nassib is the only passenger and commercial border crossing between Jordan and Syria.Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack. The Public Security Directorate (PSD) said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn.Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".

schema.headline: Jordan says 'terrorists' killed in Syria in retaliatory strike over church attack
